quotes.t: Happiness does not lie in happiness, but in the achievement of it.
Love all God's creation, the whole of it and every grain of sand in it.
Destroy my desires, eradicate my ideals, show me something better, and I will follow you.
Remember then: there is only one time that is important — Now! It is the most important time because it is the only time when we have any power.
The most necessary man is he with whom you are, for no man knows whether he will ever have dealings with any one else.
The most important affair is, to do him good, because for that purpose alone was man sent into this life!
Speech is a mirror of the soul; as a man speaks, so is he.
Every day should be passed as if it were to be our last.
Powerful indeed is the empire of habit.
A man lives by believing something; not by debating and arguing about many things.
quotes.source: On Heroes, Hero-Worship, and the Heroic in History (1841)

quotes.t: Work is the grand cure of all the maladies and miseries that ever beset mankind — honest work, which you intend getting done.
The most unhappy of all men is the man who cannot tell what he is going to do, who has got no work cut-out for him in the world, and does not go into it.
A biography is considered complete if it merely accounts for six or seven selves, whereas a person may well have as many thousand.
So that was the Lighthouse, was it? No, the other was also the Lighthouse. For nothing was simply one thing.
As long as she thinks of a man, nobody objects to a woman thinking.
I am alone and miserable; man will not associate with me.
You are my creator, but I am your master; obey!
I shall be with you on your wedding-night.
There is nothing stable in the world; uproar's your only music.
quotes.source: Letter to George and Thomas Keats, 13 January 1818

quotes.t: I have been astonished that men could die martyrs for their religion.
While we are laughing, the seed of trouble is put into the wide arable land of events.
quotes.source: Letter to George and Georgiana Keats, spring 1819

quotes.t: They cannot make history who forget history.
A just society is that society in which ascending sense of reverence and descending sense of contempt is dissolved into the creation of a compassionate society.
Unlike a drop of water which loses its identity when it joins the ocean, man does not lose his being in the society in which he lives. Man's life is independent.
The day you teach the child the name of the bird, the child will never see that bird again.
quotes.source: as quoted in Anthony de Mello, Awareness (1992)

quotes.t: Freedom and love go together. Love is not a reaction.
That is the first thing to learn — not to seek. When you seek you are really only window shopping.
He who does not understand your silence will probably not understand your words.
quotes.source: Roycroft Dictionary and Book of Epigrams (1923)

quotes.t: A man is not paid for having a head and hands, but for using them.
Life in abundance comes only through great love.
He who permits himself to tell a lie once, finds it much easier to do it a second and third time, till at length it becomes habitual.
It is neither wealth nor splendor; but tranquility and occupation which give you happiness.
quotes.source: Letter to Anna Scott Jefferson, 12 July 1788

quotes.t: I have never been able to conceive how any rational being could propose happiness to himself from the exercise of power over others.
quotes.source: Letter to A. L. C. Destutt de Tracy, 26 January 1811

quotes.t: My model for business is The Beatles: They were four guys that kept each other's kind of negative tendencies in check. They balanced each other and the total was greater than the sum of the parts. That's how I see business: great things in business are never done by one person, they're done by a team of people.

People think focus means saying yes to the thing you've got to focus on. But that's not what it means at all. It means saying no to the hundred other good ideas that there are. You have to pick carefully. I'm actually as proud of the things we haven't done as the things I have done. Innovation is saying no to 1,000 things.
Technology is nothing. What's important is that you have a faith in people, that they're basically good and smart, and if you give them tools, they'll do wonderful things with them.
There is a god within us. It is when he stirs us that our bosom warms.
I grabbed a pile of dust, and holding it up, foolishly asked for as many birthdays as the grains of dust, I forgot to ask that they be years of youth.
Everything comes gradually and at its appointed hour.
Ah, what happiness it is to be with people who all are happy, to press hands, press cheeks, smile into eyes.
How idiotic civilization is! Why be given a body if you have to keep it shut up in a case like a rare, rare fiddle?
I am poor — obscure — just eighteen years of age — with a rapacious appetite for everything and principles as light as my purse.
I have not been trampled on. I have not been petrified. I have not been buried with inferior minds, and excluded from every glimpse of communion with what is bright and energetic and high.
Life is so constructed, that the event does not, cannot, will not, match the expectation.

If people were always kind and obedient to those who are cruel and unjust, the wicked people would have it all their own way: they would never feel afraid, and so they would never alter, but would grow worse and worse.
Seeing, hearing, feeling, are miracles, and each part and tag of me is a miracle.
quotes.source: Song of Myself, section 24, Leaves of Grass

quotes.t: I think I could turn and live with animals, they are so placid and self-contain'd, I stand and look at them long and long.
quotes.source: Song of Myself, section 32, Leaves of Grass

quotes.t: From this hour I ordain myself loos'd of limits and imaginary lines.
quotes.source: Song of the Open Road, section 5, Leaves of Grass

quotes.t: If you have a garden and a library, you have everything you need.
quotes.source: Letter to Varro, Ad Familiares IX, 4, 46 BC

quotes.t: Any man is liable to a mistake; but no one but a downright fool will persist in error.
The sinews of war are infinite money.
At a time like this, scorching irony, not convincing argument, is needed.
quotes.source: What to the Slave Is the Fourth of July?, 5 July 1852

quotes.t: Interpreted as it ought to be interpreted, the Constitution is a glorious liberty document.
quotes.source: What to the Slave Is the Fourth of July?, 5 July 1852

quotes.t: What, to the American slave, is your 4th of July? I answer: a day that reveals to him, more than all other days in the year, the gross injustice and cruelty to which he is the constant victim.
quotes.source: What to the Slave Is the Fourth of July?, 5 July 1852

quotes.t: I feel no need for any other faith than my faith in human beings.
I enjoy life because I am endlessly interested in people and their growth.
I became mentally bifocal, and so I learned early to understand that there is no such condition in human affairs as absolute truth.
What a liberation to realize that the 'voice in my head' is not who I am. Who am I then? The one who sees that.
The moment you realize you are not present, you are present.
To love is to recognize yourself in another.
The age when silence is considered an indication of wisdom is over. This is an age of the people, an age of dialogue, a time when people must share their opinions and thoroughly discuss things.

Only the latter is required of the artist. Not a single problem is resolved in Anna Karenina or Eugene Onegin, and yet the novels satisfy you completely because all the problems they raise are formulated correctly.
If you learn from defeat, you haven't really lost.
It's the repetition of affirmations that leads to belief. And once that belief becomes a deep conviction, things begin to happen.
quotes.source: Muhammad Ali Center, "In His Own Words"

quotes.t: The best thinking has been done in solitude. The worst has been done in turmoil.
quotes.source: The Diary and Sundry Observations of Thomas Alva Edison (1948)

quotes.t: Sunset and evening star, and one clear call for me!
Success is something you attract by the person you become.
We must not forget that when radium was discovered no one knew that it would prove useful in hospitals. The work was one of pure science.
Let's not allow ourselves to be upset by small things we should despise and forget.
quotes.source: How to Stop Worrying and Start Living (1948)

quotes.t: I try to buy stock in businesses that are so wonderful that an idiot can run them. Because sooner or later, one will.
quotes.source: Panel discussion after the premiere of I.O.U.S.A. (2008)

quotes.t: I can testify to what UNICEF means to children, because I was among those who received food and medical relief right after World War II, I have a long-lasting gratitude and trust for what UNICEF does.
quotes.source: Statement to UNICEF (as quoted at UNICEF.org)

quotes.t: I don't believe that the public knows what it wants; this is the conclusion that I have drawn from my career.
Lives of great men all remind us we can make our lives sublime, and, departing, leave behind us footprints on the sands of time.
Happy the man, whose wish and care a few paternal acres bound, content to breathe his native air, in his own ground.
Revenge is a kind of wild justice.
What we hope ever to do with ease, we may learn first to do with diligence.
Deals are my art form. Other people paint beautifully on canvas or write wonderful poetry. I like making deals, preferably big deals. That's how I get my kicks.
quotes.source: Trump: The Art of the Deal (1987)

quotes.t: Generally speaking, the errors in religion are dangerous; those in philosophy only ridiculous.
And so rock bottom became the solid foundation on which I rebuilt my life.
Change only happens when ordinary people get involved, get engaged, and come together to demand it.
Tell your heart that the fear of suffering is worse than the suffering itself.
I want to make it clear that perfection is an impossible goal and should never be a true pursuit in life.
I have always been very confident and very upbeat about the future potential of India. I think it is a great country with great potential.
Machines take me by surprise with great frequency.
I will not serve that in which I no longer believe, whether it call itself my home, my fatherland, or my church.
quotes.source: A Portrait of the Artist as a Young Man (1916)

quotes.t: One important key to success is self-confidence. An important key to self-confidence is preparation.
It has yet to be proved that intelligence has real survival value.
The revolution is not an apple that falls when it is ripe. You have to make it fall.
quotes.source: Intercontinental Press, Vol. 3 (January-April 1965); also in Che Guevara Speaks: Selected Speeches and Writings (1967)

quotes.t: No human race is superior; no religious faith is inferior. All collective judgments are wrong. Only racists make them.
quotes.source: "Have You Learned The Most Important Lesson Of All?", Parade Magazine (24 May 1992)

quotes.t: The longest day must have its close — the gloomiest night will wear on to a morning.
I cannot stand and sing the anthem. I cannot salute the flag. I know that I am a black man in a white world.
Good manners is the art of making those people easy with whom we converse.
quotes.source: A Treatise on Good Manners and Good Breeding (1754, published posthumously)

quotes.t: The world begins at a kitchen table. No matter what, we must eat to live.
quotes.source: "Perhaps the World Ends Here", The Woman Who Fell from the Sky (1994)

quotes.t: I will tell you something about stories. They aren't just entertainment. Don't be fooled. They are all we have, you see, all we have to fight off illness and death.
The only lasting truth is change.
quotes.source: Parable of the Sower (1993), ch. 1 (Earthseed verse)

quotes.t: There are only two ways to influence human behavior: you can manipulate it or you can inspire it.
A man's not dead while his name is still spoken.
Out of the crooked timber of humanity, no straight thing was ever made.
quotes.source: Idea for a Universal History with a Cosmopolitan Purpose (1784), Proposition 6

quotes.t: The mind once enlightened cannot again become dark.
quotes.source: A Letter Addressed to the Abbe Raynal (1782)

quotes.t: We need to respect the oceans and take care of them as if our lives depended on it. Because they do.
quotes.source: "My wish: Protect our oceans", TED Prize talk (February 2009)

Alan Turing.bio: English mathematician and father of computer science; cracked the Enigma code in WWII.

Alexander Pope.bio: English poet and master of the heroic couplet. His works include An Essay on Criticism, The Rape of the Lock and An Essay on Man, along with celebrated translations of Homer.

Alfred Tennyson.bio: English Poet Laureate; author of In Memoriam and Ulysses.

Anton Chekhov.bio: Anton Chekhov was a Russian playwright and master of the short story, a practising doctor who wrote The Cherry Orchard, Uncle Vanya and hundreds of stories. His restrained, humane art reshaped both the theatre and short fiction of the 20th century.

Arthur C. Clarke.bio: British science-fiction writer (1917–2008), author of 2001: A Space Odyssey.

Audrey Hepburn.bio: Audrey Hepburn was a British actress and humanitarian celebrated for films such as Roman Holiday, Breakfast at Tiffany's and My Fair Lady. In later life she devoted herself to UNICEF, serving as a Goodwill Ambassador in some of the world's poorest regions.

B.R. Ambedkar.bio: Indian jurist and social reformer who chaired the drafting of India's Constitution and campaigned against caste discrimination.

Barack Obama.bio: 44th president of the United States (2009-2017), the first African American to hold the office; Nobel Peace Prize 2009.

Charlie Chaplin.bio: Charlie Chaplin was an English comic actor and filmmaker whose Little Tramp became a global icon of silent cinema. He co-founded United Artists and wrote, directed and starred in classics including City Lights, Modern Times and The Great Dictator.

Charlotte Brontë.bio: English novelist, author of Jane Eyre.
Charlotte Brontë.credit: Alonzo Chappel, Public domain (File: File:Charlotte Bronte by Alonzo Chappel.jpg)

Che Guevara.bio: Argentine Marxist revolutionary, physician and writer whose journeys across Latin America, recorded in The Motorcycle Diaries, shaped his convictions. A major figure of the Cuban Revolution, his essays and speeches remain widely read and debated.

Cicero.bio: Marcus Tullius Cicero was a Roman statesman, lawyer and orator considered the master of Latin prose. His speeches, letters and philosophical works, including On Friendship, transmitted Greek philosophy to the Roman world.

Daisaku Ikeda.bio: Daisaku Ikeda was a Japanese Buddhist philosopher, educator and peace activist who led the Soka Gakkai lay Buddhist movement and founded Soka University. He wrote extensively on Buddhism, dialogue and peace.

Dale Carnegie.bio: Dale Carnegie was an American writer and lecturer on self-improvement and public speaking. His book How to Win Friends and Influence People (1936) became one of the best-selling books of all time.

David Hume.bio: David Hume was a Scottish Enlightenment philosopher, historian and economist, best known for A Treatise of Human Nature and An Enquiry Concerning Human Understanding. His scepticism about causation, miracles and the self profoundly influenced Western philosophy.

Donald Trump.bio: Donald Trump is an American businessman and television personality who served as the 45th President of the United States (2017–2021) and was elected again as the 47th President in 2024. Before politics he built a real-estate business and hosted the reality show The Apprentice.

Eckhart Tolle.bio: Eckhart Tolle is a German-born spiritual teacher living in Canada, author of The Power of Now (1997) and A New Earth (2005), books on presence and the ego that became international bestsellers.

Elbert Hubbard.bio: Elbert Hubbard was an American writer, publisher and philosopher who founded the Roycroft arts-and-crafts community. His essay "A Message to Garcia" (1899) was one of the most widely reprinted works of its era; he died in the sinking of the Lusitania.

Elie Wiesel.bio: Romanian-born American writer (1928–2016), author of Night.

Francis Bacon.bio: Francis Bacon was an English philosopher, statesman and essayist who championed the empirical method of inquiry. His Essays and his plan for the reform of learning in the Novum Organum helped lay the groundwork of modern science.

Frederick Douglass.bio: American abolitionist and writer who escaped slavery and became a leading voice against it.

Fyodor Dostoevsky.bio: Russian novelist, author of Crime and Punishment and The Brothers Karamazov.

Harriet Beecher Stowe.bio: Harriet Beecher Stowe was an American author and abolitionist whose novel Uncle Tom's Cabin (1852) galvanized anti-slavery sentiment in the United States and abroad. She wrote more than 30 books, including novels, travel memoirs and collections of articles.

Henry Wadsworth Longfellow.bio: Henry Wadsworth Longfellow was an American poet and educator, among the most popular poets of his century. He wrote Paul Revere's Ride, The Song of Hiawatha and Evangeline, and produced the first American translation of Dante's Divine Comedy.

Immanuel Kant.bio: Immanuel Kant was a German philosopher whose Critique of Pure Reason reshaped modern philosophy by examining the limits of human knowledge. His moral philosophy grounded duty in reason and human dignity, and his essays championed enlightenment and perpetual peace.
Immanuel Kant.credit: J. L. Raab, after a painting by Döbler, Public domain

J.K. Rowling.bio: British author (1965– ), creator of Harry Potter.

Jackie Robinson.bio: American baseball player (1919–1972), the first African American to play in Major League Baseball.

James Joyce.bio: Irish novelist, author of Ulysses, a landmark of modernist literature.

Jiddu Krishnamurti.bio: Indian philosopher and speaker on the nature of mind, meditation, and human freedom; rejected all guru roles.

Jim Rohn.bio: Emanuel James Rohn, known as Jim Rohn, was an American entrepreneur and motivational speaker whose seminars and books on personal development influenced a generation of speakers, including Tony Robbins.

John Keats.bio: English Romantic poet of the great Odes, including Ode to a Nightingale.

Jonathan Swift.bio: Anglo-Irish writer and satirist, author of Thoughts on Various Subjects.

Joy Harjo.bio: Muscogee (Creek) poet, musician and author who served three terms as United States Poet Laureate, the first Native American to hold the post. Poems such as Remember call readers back to sky, earth and ancestry.

Katherine Mansfield.bio: New Zealand modernist short-story writer, a leading figure of early 20th-century literature alongside Joyce and Woolf.
Katherine Mansfield.credit: Archives New Zealand from New Zealand, CC BY-SA 2.0

Leo Tolstoy.bio: Russian novelist, author of War and Peace and Anna Karenina.

Leslie Marmon Silko.bio: Laguna Pueblo novelist and storyteller whose Ceremony (1977) is a central work of Native American literature. Her writing weaves story, land, memory and healing into a single fabric, in the Pueblo oral tradition.

Marie Curie.bio: Marie Curie was a Polish-born physicist and chemist who pioneered the study of radioactivity, a term she coined. She remains the only person to win Nobel Prizes in two different sciences — Physics in 1903 and Chemistry in 1911 — and died of illness caused by her long exposure to radiation.

Mary Shelley.bio: English novelist, author of Frankenstein, a founding work of science fiction.

Muhammad Ali.bio: American heavyweight boxing champion and cultural icon known as much for his activism as his titles.

Ovid.bio: Ovid was a Roman poet celebrated for the Metamorphoses, a vast narrative poem of mythological transformations. Exiled by the emperor Augustus to the Black Sea coast, he spent his last decade writing poems of lament and endurance.

Paulo Coelho.bio: Brazilian lyricist and novelist whose novel The Alchemist became one of the best-selling books in history, translated into dozens of languages. His fables about following one's dreams have inspired readers on every continent.

Pearl Buck.bio: Pearl S. Buck was an American writer who spent much of her early life in China, where her parents were missionaries. Her novel The Good Earth won the Pulitzer Prize, and she received the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1938.

Publilius Syrus.bio: Publilius Syrus was a Latin writer of the 1st century BC who was brought to Italy as a slave from Syria and later freed. He is known for his Sententiae, a collection of moral maxims drawn from his mimes.

Ratan Tata.role: Industrialist, chairman emeritus of Tata Sons
Ratan Tata.bio: Chairman of Tata Sons for more than two decades, Ratan Tata transformed the Tata group into a global conglomerate with acquisitions such as Tetley, Corus and Jaguar Land Rover. Revered in India for his integrity and philanthropy, he also championed the Tata Nano, the world's cheapest car.

Samuel Johnson.bio: Samuel Johnson was an English writer who compiled the first great Dictionary of the English Language in 1755. Poet, essayist and the most quoted conversationalist of his age, his life was immortalised in Boswell's famous biography.

Serena Williams.bio: American tennis legend who won 23 Grand Slam singles titles, the most in the Open Era, along with four Olympic gold medals. Born in Saginaw, Michigan, and raised in Compton, California, she dominated women's tennis for over two decades and became a successful businesswoman and advocate for women.

Simon Sinek.bio: British-American author and speaker (born 1973), known for the book Start With Why and his 2009 TEDx talk on inspirational leadership.

Steve Jobs.bio: Co-founder of Apple, Steve Jobs helped launch the personal computer era and later reinvented music, phones and tablets with the iPod, iPhone and iPad. Forced out of Apple in 1985, he founded NeXT and built Pixar into a major studio before returning in 1997 to rescue the company he had started.

Sylvia Earle.bio: American marine biologist and oceanographer (born 1935), known as 'Her Deepness'.

Terry Pratchett.bio: English author (1948–2015), creator of the Discworld series.

Thomas Carlyle.bio: Thomas Carlyle was a Scottish historian, philosopher and essayist whose works, including Sartor Resartus and On Heroes, Hero-Worship, and the Heroic in History, shaped Victorian thought. His history of the French Revolution is regarded as a classic of the genre.

Thomas Edison.bio: Thomas Edison was an American inventor who developed the phonograph, the motion picture camera and the first practical electric light bulb. He held over a thousand US patents and founded the first industrial research laboratory at Menlo Park, New Jersey.

Thomas Jefferson.bio: Thomas Jefferson was an American statesman and Founding Father who wrote the Declaration of Independence and served as the third President of the United States (1801–1809). He founded the University of Virginia and doubled the nation's size with the Louisiana Purchase.

Thomas Paine.bio: Thomas Paine was an English-born political writer whose pamphlet Common Sense in 1776 galvanised the American Revolution. His Rights of Man defended the French Revolution against Burke, and his works made him one of the most influential pamphleteers in history.

Virginia Woolf.bio: Virginia Woolf was an English writer and a central figure of literary modernism, famous for stream-of-consciousness novels such as Mrs Dalloway (1925) and To the Lighthouse (1927). Her essay A Room of One's Own (1929) became a foundational feminist text on women and writing. With her husband Leonard she founded the Hogarth Press, which published her own work and that of T. S. Eliot and others.

Walt Whitman.bio: American poet best known for the collection Leaves of Grass (1855).

Warren Buffett.bio: Investor Warren Buffett, the 'Oracle of Omaha', turned Berkshire Hathaway into one of the world's largest conglomerates through patient, disciplined value investing. Famous for his annual shareholder letters and frugal personal habits, he has pledged to give away the great majority of his fortune.

Zig Ziglar.bio: Zig Ziglar was an American author and motivational speaker who became one of the most influential sales and personal-development trainers of the twentieth century. His book See You at the Top and his famous line 'Your attitude, not your aptitude, will determine your altitude' reached millions.
